content: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.

I'll begin by understanding what you're really after, before anything technical.

You said you want to save and manage bookmarks. Let me start with the *why*:

**When this app is finished and working well, what would be different from how you handle bookmarks today?** What problem are you feeling right now that made you want to build this?

For example — are your bookmarks scattered and hard to find again? Are you saving lots of links but never coming back to them? Something else entirely?

A second thing to help me picture it: **what kind of bookmarks are these mostly** — web pages you want to read later, tools/sites you return to often, references for a project, or a mix?

I'll hold off on any technical questions and screens until I understand the goal. Once I do, I'll show you a working screen you can actually click through, one step at a time.

Right now my bookmarks are scattered across browser folders and I often can’t find something when I need it. I also save things to read later, then lose track of what I’ve actually read.

They’re a mix of articles, useful tools, and project references. I’d like one place where I can save a link quickly, organise it with tags, search for it later, and keep a clear read-later list.

That's clear. Let me play back what I understand and check I've got the *core* right.

**What I heard:** Today your bookmarks are scattered across browser folders, so when you actually need something you can't find it. And for things you save to read later, you lose track of what you've already read versus what's still waiting.

So the real goal isn't just "store links" — it's **being able to reliably find a saved link again, and having a clear picture of your read-later pile.** The saving, tagging, and searching are the *means* to that. Does that match how you see it?

One scope question to make sure I aim at the heart of it: if I had to name the single biggest win, would it be **"I can always find a link when I need it"**, or **"I finally stay on top of my read-later list"** — or are those genuinely equal in importance to you?

I'll take your answer, confirm the goal, and then move on to the kind of app you have in mind before I show you anything on screen.
Yes, that matches. Finding saved links again is the biggest win. The read-later list is important too, but secondary.

**What kind of app do you have in mind?** For example:
- **Web app** — you open it in a browser, works on any computer
- **Mobile app** — on your phone
- **Desktop app** — an installed program on your computer
- **Terminal/command-line** — text-based

Since a lot of bookmark-saving happens while you're browsing, web is a common fit — but I want your preference, not my assumption. Which feels right to you?
A web app feels right. I want to open it in a browser and use it comfortably on both my computer and phone.

**Open this in your browser: http://maker:4001**

You'll see a screen titled "My Bookmarks" with a box at the top and an empty list below.

**Flow 1 — saving a link.** Please do this one action: click into the input box, paste (or type) any web link you'd actually save — for example `https://example.com/some-article` — and click **Save link**.

You should see the link appear immediately at the top of a "Saved links" list, with a name shown above the address.

A couple of things I decided for you here, which I'd like you to judge:
- I made the app **show a name/title for each link** (guessed from the address) so you can recognise it later, rather than showing only the raw web address. Does having a readable name matter to you, or would the address alone be enough?
- I put the **newest saved link at the top** of the list. Is newest-first the order you'd expect?

Go ahead and save a link — then tell me: does that saving experience match what you had in mind?

Mostly, yes—the link appearing immediately feels right, and newest-first is what I’d expect. A readable name matters a lot, but I’d want the app to pick up the page’s actual title rather than guessing it from the address, with a way for me to change it if needed.

1. Save a link (or use one already there).

- Tagging happens **per link on its card**, not during the initial save.

Please refresh **http://maker:4001**. Make sure you have a few links saved, some with tags. Then let's find things:

1. **Search by words:** type part of a title or address into the new **"Search by title, address, or tag"** box. The list narrows as you type to only matching links, and the count shows e.g. *"1 of 4"*. Click **Clear** to see everything again.
2. **Search finds tags too:** type a tag word (e.g. `article`) — links carrying that tag match as well.
3. **Filter by clicking a tag:** click a **tag chip** on any link. The list narrows to just links with that tag, and a banner appears: *"Filtered by tag … — show all"*. Click **show all** to reset.
4. **No matches:** search for something nonsense like `zzzz` — you get a friendly *"No links match your search"* message instead of a blank screen.

What I decided for you here, for your judgement:
- Search looks across **title, web address, and tags together** (one box, not separate fields), matching as you type.
- I made **tag chips clickable** as a quick one-tap filter, shown separately from the typed search, with a clear way back to the full list.

Does this finding-and-filtering behaviour match how you'd want to locate a saved link?
Yes, this feels straightforward and sufficient for finding a saved link. I like having one search box, clickable tag filters, a visible count, and an obvious way to return to the full list.

Please refresh **http://maker:4001**. Let's walk the read-later flow:

1. Notice each saved link now shows its reading status — a new link starts as **"● To read"** with a **"Mark as read"** button.
2. On one link, click **Mark as read**. Its status flips to **"✓ Read"**, the card dims slightly, and the button now offers **"Mark as to read"** so you can undo it.
3. Up top there are three view tabs: **All**, **To read**, and **Read**. Click **To read** — you see only your unread pile, and notice the little number badge on that tab counts how many are still to read. Click **Read** to see what you've finished, and **All** to see everything.

What I decided for you, for your judgement:
- Every saved link is **"To read" by default** when you save it, on the assumption a freshly-saved link hasn't been read yet.
- I put the reading pile behind **three simple views (All / To read / Read)** with an **unread count badge**, rather than, say, hiding read items automatically.
- Read items stay in the list but look **slightly dimmed**, and marking read is fully reversible.

Does this read-later behaviour match how you'd want to track what you've read?

The views, count, and reversible read status feel right. I wouldn’t want every saved link to start as “To read,” though, because tools and reference links aren’t necessarily reading material. I’d like to choose whether a link goes into the read-later list when I save it, and still be able to change that afterward.

1. **Save a reference/tool link *without* read-later:** paste a link, leave the new checkbox *"Add this to my read-later list"* **unchecked**, and Save. On its card you'll see it's *not* in the reading pile — just a **"+ Add to read-later"** button, no "To read" status.
2. **Save something to read:** paste another link, **tick** the checkbox, and Save. This one shows **"● To read"** with **"Mark as read"**.
3. **Change your mind later, both ways:** on the reference link, click **"+ Add to read-later"** — it now joins the pile as "To read". On a read-later link, click **"Remove from read-later"** — it drops out of the pile.
4. Check the **To read** tab and its count — only links you chose for read-later appear there; your tools/references don't clutter it.

What I set up for your judgement:
- The read-later checkbox is **unchecked by default**, so a link only enters your reading pile when you deliberately opt in.
- Links outside read-later show **no reading status at all** (just the quick "+ Add" option), keeping tools and references clean.

1. **Save a link in seconds** — paste an address and it's stored; the app fetches the page's real name so you recognise it, and you can rename it anytime (even if the name can't be fetched, it's still saved).
2. **Organise with tags** — add your own tag words to any link, and as you type it suggests tags you've already used so you stay consistent instead of creating near-duplicates.
3. **Find anything fast** — one search box across names, addresses, and tags, plus one-tap filtering by clicking a tag, with a clear count and an easy way back to the full list. *(This is your biggest win.)*
4. **Keep a real read-later list** — choose which links are reading material, mark them read/unread, and switch between All / To read / Read views with an unread count. Tools and references stay out of the reading pile.
5. **Manage the collection** — delete a bookmark (with a confirm step), no duplicate copies (you're taken to the existing one to edit), long names wrap so they're readable, friendly empty states, and everything you save is still there when you return.

I've also noted your wish for it to feel **comfortable on both computer and phone** to handle when we polish the look.

That's 8 settled flows covering your goal. **May I now start building this for real?** (That moves us out of exploration and into implementation.)

content:
Everything is built and verified. Switching to Phase 4 (acceptance).

## Verification report

I ran the checks against every approved behaviour, plus internal quality tests — **all 19 passed**:

- **Saving & titles (SCN-001):** valid links save, the real page title is fetched, newest appears first, renaming works.
- **Tags (SCN-002):** free-form, lower-cased, de-duplicated, removable.
- **Finding (SCN-003):** one search box across title/address/tags, plus tag-click filtering, with counts.
- **Read-later (SCN-004):** opt-in at save, read/unread toggle, All/To read/Read views, unread badge; leaving read-later clears read.
- **Edge cases (SCN-005):** friendly empty states, invalid input rejected, a page whose title can't be fetched still saves and shows the address.
- **Duplicates (SCN-006):** no second copy — you're taken to the existing bookmark to edit.
- **Delete (SCN-007):** confirm step, then it's gone everywhere including the unread count.
- **Long text & persistence (SCN-008):** long names wrap; a dedicated test confirms your bookmarks (titles, tags, read-later status) survive closing and reopening.

## Try the real app

**It's running at → http://maker:4000**

This is the actual application (not the prototype): it saves to real storage that persists, and it fetches real page titles over the network. One honest note — if a particular website can't be reached from this environment, that bookmark will simply fall back to showing its address with the "couldn't fetch title" note, exactly as we agreed; the save still succeeds.

Please have a look and use it as you would for real — save a few links, tag and search them, try the read-later views.
